chunk_findings.detail: Decision 1 promises that "the default template for each kind reproduces today's ids exactly", and Decision 2 calls the token set "the full set" — but the token set `{prefix} {seq} {date} {slug} {hash} {parent} {phase} {env} {user-text}` has no token for the pid, while the Context explicitly lists `services/sessions.new_session_id` as an id minted today with shape `s<UTC timestamp>-<pid>`. The session default therefore cannot be expressed with the listed tokens, so the "sees no change / replay byte-identically" guarantee is false for sessions. Worse, the validation rule ("a template that could produce the same id twice without `{seq}` or `{hash}` refused") would reject the session default outright, because `s{date}-…` contains neither `{seq}` nor `{hash}`; a project that "sets nothing" and inherits the documented default would fail validation. Either the token set must gain the missing token, or the default/validation claims must be narrowed.

chunk_findings.detail: Decision 3 says that on an offline clash "the record that is later in the fold order keeps its id unchanged and gains the alias `<id>.<clone suffix>` … Nothing is renumbered." Since aliases are additive (Decision 4: ids are never renamed), the earlier colliding record also retains the id `BUG-123`. Two records therefore end up with the same canonical id `BUG-123`, and the disambiguating alias `BUG-123.b` is attached to the other (winning) record, not the loser: a lookup of `BUG-123` still resolves to two records, and a lookup of `BUG-123.b` returns the record that already had the plain id, i.e. the alias cannot be used to reach the losing record. This contradicts the stated goal that a clash "produces a visible suffix, not a silent duplicate." Concretely, two clones minting `BUG-123` offline and then merging leave an ambiguous `BUG-123`, which `show`/doctor cannot resolve. Either the losing record's canonical lookup key must become the suffixed name (a rename, which Decision 4 forbids) or the alias must be attached to the losing record, and the doc does not say how the two same-id records are told apart.

chunk_findings.detail: The rule now declares a template valid if it contains "at least one source of uniqueness: `{seq}`, `{hash}`, `{digest}` (deliberately stable), or `{time}` together with `{pid}`." But the preceding sentence in the same item defines `{digest}` as a deterministic content digest whose whole point is that "the same failing check maps to the same bug," i.e. filing the same text twice yields ONE id, not two. So the example template `Bci-{slug}-{digest}` — which the text itself presents as a shipped default — satisfies the "uniqueness" requirement while doing exactly what the original rule forbade ("a template that could produce the same id twice without `{seq}` or `{hash}` refused"). Listing `{digest}` among the uniqueness sources makes the validation rule self-contradictory: a template consisting only of `{digest}` (plus `{slug}`/`{prefix}`) is accepted, yet it can mint a duplicate key for identical content. Either `{digest}` must not count as a uniqueness source, or it needs an explicit, separate carve-out for the deliberately-stable CI-bug case.

chunk_findings.detail:
The rewritten validation rule accepts any template that "must declare `stable = true`" when it lacks `{seq}`, `{hash}`, or `{time}`+`{pid}`, but it never requires a stable template to actually contain a content-determined token (`{digest}`). It only imposes the converse ("`{digest}` is allowed only in stable templates"). Two concrete cases fall through:

1. Volatile token in a "stable" template: config `template = "{prefix}-{date}"` (or `"{prefix}-{time}"`, `"{prefix}-{pid}"`) has no listed uniqueness source, so it satisfies the rule by declaring `stable = true`. Yet `{date}`/`{time}`/`{pid}` change between filings, so filing identical content the next day produces a different id. This directly contradicts the next sentence, "A stable template maps the same content to the same id on purpose, so filing it again extends the existing record instead of creating a new one." The pre-change rule refused this template; the change now admits it.

2. Colliding "stable" template: config `template = "B{slug}"` with `stable = true` is admitted, and two different reports that happen to share a slug map to the same id, silently extending an unrelated record. Since the rule does not require `{digest}` (or any deterministic content token) in stable templates, the stated guarantee ("maps the same content to the same id") is not enforced in either direction.

A correct rule would require stable templates to contain `{digest}` and to exclude volatile tokens (`{date}`, `{time}`, `{pid}`, `{env}`, `{hash}`), e.g. `Bci-{slug}-{digest}`. As written, a config that passes validation can violate the semantic the paragraph claims for it.

chunk_findings.detail: The clash rule silently renames a user-visible id, contradicting both the same paragraph ("No event changes, and nothing is renumbered or renamed") and decision 4 ("A recorded id is never renamed"). The key is explicitly defined as "the record's KEY, which is what people see and type and what ddflow prints"; the later record's key being "shown as `BUG-123.<clone suffix>`" is therefore a rename, not an alias. Concrete scenario: clone A and clone B both work offline and each file a bug, so both mint key `BUG-123`. B's users type `BUG-123` into a commit message. After the logs meet, B's record is reassigned the key `BUG-123.b`, and the string `BUG-123` in B's commit now resolves to A's record. The doc's own remedy for disagreements is "aliases only" (decision 4), but no alias is used; the loser's printed id is changed. The statement that nothing is renamed is false.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/decisions/id-schemes.md — section 3 "Sequential numbers" (clash handling)

chunk_findings.detail: The rule accepts `{time}`+`{pid}` as "a source of uniqueness," but `{time}` is defined two bullets earlier as "UTC timestamp, second resolution." Two records minted by the same process within one calendar second therefore produce identical keys, so the rule does not guarantee uniqueness. Concrete input: a project sets `[ids] task = "T-{time}-{pid}"`; the validation accepts it as unique; a script then creates two tasks in the same second from the same process, and both get key `T-20261005120000-4242`. This also undercuts the claim "All agents on one machine share the log, so a key is unique there" and "Each shipped default passes these rules" (the session default `s{time}-{pid}` has exactly this collision window).

chunk_findings.detail: The new sentences say the id service "checks every key it mints against every id and key of every kind in the folded log ... A key that is already taken gets `-2`, `-3`, and so on." Two sentences later the doc keeps: "A stable template maps the same content to the same id on purpose, so filing it again extends the existing record instead of creating a new one." These two rules give contradictory outcomes for the *same* condition ("the key I just computed is already in the log"): the new rule says mint a new, suffixed key (`…-2`), the stable rule says reuse/extend the existing record. Concrete input: a stable template such as `note-{slug}` with `stable = true`; file it once (record gets key `note-foo`), then file identical content again. The second filing computes `note-foo`, the check finds it "already taken", and the new rule produces a second record whose key is `note-foo-2` instead of extending the first — breaking the idempotency the stable paragraph promises. Unless the check is explicitly carved out for stable templates (the diff does not say so, and it says "every key it mints"), the two adjacent rules conflict and the doc no longer tells an implementer which branch wins.

chunk_findings.detail: The clash rule silently renames a user-visible id, contradicting both the same paragraph ("No event changes, and nothing is renumbered or renamed") and decision 4 ("A recorded id is never renamed"). The key is explicitly defined as "the record's KEY, which is what people see and type and what ddflow prints"; the later record's key being "shown as `BUG-123.<clone suffix>`" is therefore a rename, not an alias. Concrete scenario: clone A and clone B both work offline and each file a bug, so both mint key `BUG-123`. B's users type `BUG-123` into a commit message. After the logs meet, B's record is reassigned the key `BUG-123.b`, and the string `BUG-123` in B's commit now resolves to A's record. The doc's own remedy for disagreements is "aliases only" (decision 4), but no alias is used; the loser's printed id is changed. The statement that nothing is renamed is false.

chunk_findings.detail: The rule accepts `{time}`+`{pid}` as "a source of uniqueness," but `{time}` is defined two bullets earlier as "UTC timestamp, second resolution." Two records minted by the same process within one calendar second therefore produce identical keys, so the rule does not guarantee uniqueness. Concrete input: a project sets `[ids] task = "T-{time}-{pid}"`; the validation accepts it as unique; a script then creates two tasks in the same second from the same process, and both get key `T-20261005120000-4242`. This also undercuts the claim "All agents on one machine share the log, so a key is unique there" and "Each shipped default passes these rules" (the session default `s{time}-{pid}` has exactly this collision window).

chunk_findings.detail: `{seq}` is allocated "for that kind" (per-kind counter), and the validation rule only requires that the template contain one of `{seq}`, `{hash}`, or `{time}`+`{pid}`; nothing requires a token that distinguishes kinds. So the validation admits configs where two different kinds mint the same key. Concrete input: `[ids] task = "{seq}"` and `[ids] bug = "{seq}"`; the first task and first bug both get key `1`. The doc nevertheless asserts that a key "is unique there" and that a key can be resolved to the internal id before recording; with a non-unique key, `ddflow show 1` (accepting a bare key) resolves to two records, so the resolution contract cannot hold. The validation that is supposed to make every template legal does not prevent this.

chunk_findings.detail: The new sentences say the id service "checks every key it mints against every id and key of every kind in the folded log ... A key that is already taken gets `-2`, `-3`, and so on." Two sentences later the doc keeps: "A stable template maps the same content to the same id on purpose, so filing it again extends the existing record instead of creating a new one." These two rules give contradictory outcomes for the *same* condition ("the key I just computed is already in the log"): the new rule says mint a new, suffixed key (`…-2`), the stable rule says reuse/extend the existing record. Concrete input: a stable template such as `note-{slug}` with `stable = true`; file it once (record gets key `note-foo`), then file identical content again. The second filing computes `note-foo`, the check finds it "already taken", and the new rule produces a second record whose key is `note-foo-2` instead of extending the first — breaking the idempotency the stable paragraph promises. Unless the check is explicitly carved out for stable templates (the diff does not say so, and it says "every key it mints"), the two adjacent rules conflict and the doc no longer tells an implementer which branch wins.

chunk_findings.detail: `{hash}` is defined as "the salted hash of `auto_id`", but Decision 1 requires the default template for each kind to reproduce today's ids byte-identically, and the auto id is `{prefix}` + ten hex digits of the salted hash of the *text* (e.g. `B9c56de9d58`). If `{hash}` really hashes `auto_id` (which already contains those ten hex digits), the default template `{prefix}{hash}` renders `B` + `salted_hash("B9c56de9d58")`, not `B9c56de9d58`. That breaks the two central promises of the change ("the default template for each kind reproduces today's ids exactly" and "existing logs replay byte-identically"). Either `{hash}` must be defined as the hash *body* of `auto_id` (the ten hex digits themselves, salted from the text), or the auto-id default cannot be written as a template. As written, a conforming implementation of the default produces different ids.

chunk_findings.detail: The uniqueness rule states the id service checks a minted key "against every id and key of every kind in the folded log", and that "keys share one namespace across kinds", while §4 says any record "may carry aliases … accepted everywhere an id is accepted" and Consequences says keys are "the same mechanism as aliases". Aliases are therefore part of the same resolution space, but the mint-time collision check enumerates only ids and keys — not aliases — and there is no rule anywhere for a key colliding with an alias. Concrete input: an existing record R carries the project label/alias `BUG-123` (exactly the JIRA-style form the doc is trying to enable); later, a kind with template `BUG-{seq}` reaches seq 123 and mints key `BUG-123`, because no id-or-key collision exists. Now `show BUG-123` matches two candidates (R via alias, the new record via key), and unlike the cross-clone key ambiguity — which is explicitly defined to refuse with exit 3 and list candidates — there is no defined outcome here. The check must include aliases, or aliases must be excluded from the key namespace, otherwise the "no silent ambiguous reference" guarantee is not met.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change puts aliases into the same "taken key" namespace that §3's stable-template exception operates on, and the two rules then disagree about what a collision means. §3 (as amended) says the service "checks every key it mints against every id, key **and alias**," and the very next sentence says that when a key "is already taken" the filing "extends that record." §4, however, says a minted key that collides with an alias "gets a suffix, like any taken key." For a stable template these are mutually exclusive outcomes, and neither section scopes the exception to id/key collisions only.

Concrete failure: record R has id `Bfoo`; later a stable template `{prefix}{slug}` is used for a check whose slug is `foo`, giving key `Bfoo`. Filing that check is supposed to be idempotent (the "taken key IS the expected match" case). Now suppose a different record R2 carries the alias `Bfoo` (permitted, since at add time `Bfoo` was not yet any id/key/alias, or the alias arrived via a clone merge, which §4 explicitly allows). The mint now sees `Bfoo` as "taken" — by R2's alias — and §3 tells it to treat that as a match and "extend that record," i.e. extend R2, which is not the stable template's record. If instead §4 is followed, it mints `Bfoo-2`, silently breaking the stable template's idempotency (the next filing mints `Bfoo-3`, and so on). The decision doc records no rule resolving this, so implementers will apply the stable-template branch first (it is stated as the exception) and corrupt the wrong record, or apply the alias branch and make stable templates non-stable. Either reading is wrong for the same input; §4 needs to carve the stable-template case out of "any taken key," or §3 needs to state that the expected match applies only to collisions with an existing *id/key* of the same template, never with an alias.

data.decision: Operator answers 2026-10-05 (next-free sequence with suffix on clash; full token set; aliases only; vocabulary also as CLI/MCP names), made precise by review: (1) [ids] template per kind, defaults reproduce today's ids exactly ({prefix}{hash} = auto_id's salted blake2b hex; sessions s{time}-{pid}; CI bugs Bci-{slug}-{digest} stable). (2) Tokens {prefix} {seq} {date} {slug} {hash} {parent} {phase} {env} {user-text} plus {time} {pid} {digest}; a template needs {seq}, {hash} or {time}+{pid}, else stable=true, which requires {digest} and only content/kind-fixed tokens. (3) Every record keeps an internal id (minted as today) that events use; {seq} templates produce a KEY resolved to it. Ids, keys and aliases share one namespace; the id service checks each minted key against all of them under the log lock and suffixes a taken key -2, -3; a stable template extends only a same-kind key match and refuses any other collision. (4) Offline clone clash: recorded keys unchanged; the bare key becomes ambiguous (refused, exit 3, candidates listed); both printed with clone suffixes; doctor lists ambiguous free-text references. Caller-named ids keep the CONTESTED/resolve flow. (5) Recorded ids never renamed; aliases on any record; alias adds refused when the name is taken; no bulk migration. (6) [vocabulary] words in human text and as aliases for CLI commands and MCP tools (calls by alias always accepted; advertised only when the tier allows); event kinds, JSON keys and canonical tool names unchanged. Full text: docs/ddflow/decisions/id-schemes.md.

data.summary: core/flowsignals.reviewer_latency_ratio takes the median of (review gate outcome ts - gate.started ts) over 30 min, divided by a 7-day median. That interval includes the agent's triage and fixes between rounds, gates recorded by hand after triage, and diff size (delta reviews of 560-695k chars after merging main). It does not measure how long the reviewer took to answer. Observed 2026-10-06: 'parallel: 2 (auto: ceiling 8; limited by reviewer latency ratio)' while the deepseek vLLM server reported 3 running, 0 waiting and 0.1% KV cache, i.e. nearly idle. Fix: measure reviewer service time per chunk (the durations ddflow review already records per chunk), normalised by chunk size, and treat it as saturation only when it rises while the reviewer's in-flight count is high; where the server exposes queue metrics (vLLM /metrics num_requests_waiting), prefer them. Regression test: long triage gaps and large diffs at constant per-chunk service time must not raise the ratio.
data.title: reviewer_latency_ratio measures wall time from gate.started to the gate outcome, not reviewer service time: an idle reviewer server shrinks parallelism

data.summary: Reported by U3 on 2026-10-06. After 'git merge main' into an item branch, 'ddflow review <id> --delta' diffs from the last reviewed head to HEAD. That range includes every commit that came in from main, so the reviewer gets 560-695k characters of other items' code, already reviewed elsewhere, instead of the item's own change. It wastes reviewer capacity, inflates review latency and produces findings about other agents' code (refuted by hand). Agents worked around it with --commit. Fix: the delta should be (merge-base(HEAD, main) .. HEAD) minus what was already reviewed, i.e. exclude commits reachable from main (git diff with --first-parent or a range diff against main's merged commits). Regression test: review, merge main with unrelated changes, delta-review: only the item's own new changes are sent.

data.question: What must change architecturally so ddflow upgrades smoothly, minor or major (like P-unify), across event log, derived stores, config, CLI/MCP/JSON interfaces and the artifacts adopted into user projects, including mixed-version clones?

(2) An older ddflow meeting data written by a newer one writes what it understands and preserves everything it does not understand untouched (unknown keys, sections, fields, regions, event kinds); it is refused (exit 3, 'upgrade ddflow to >= X') only on a DIRECT CONFLICT: a write that would lose, overwrite or downgrade content a newer version wrote (e.g. re-rendering a managed file stamped by a newer ddflow, rewriting a config section in a newer format, minting ids under a scheme it cannot apply). INTERFACES: CLI commands and flags, MCP tools, arguments and result fields, --json fields, config keys and values, event kinds and payload fields, export template data (schema_version), prompt template variables, hook commands written into projects, on-disk formats (log, local stores, generated files). For each, define what counts as additive (allowed in any release), deprecating (alias plus notice, kept until 1.0 per D-compat) and breaking (needs a declared migration and a minor bump while 0.x). Introduce FORMAT_LEVEL, an integer bumped by any change older code cannot read or write safely, separate from __version__. publish.yml stops patch-bumping everything: the bump level comes from the upgrade manifest (B-upgrade.2). release.sh fails when a surface snapshot changed without a manifest entry (snapshots in B-uni-compat-tests).
data.title: Compatibility contract: what is an interface, how each kind of change is classified (additive, deprecating, breaking), versioning by impact with a separate format level, written down and enforced by the release check

data.body: Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). Command, Param and the MCP tool spec gain aliases plus deprecated_since, replacement and removed_in (removed_in must be >= 1.0, enforced). Calling by an alias works and prints one notice per session: on stderr for the CLI, as a note in the MCP result. Aliases are hidden from --help and tools/list but always callable, and an MCP call to an unknown tool or argument suggests the closest name. Knob metadata gains renamed_from: the old key is read with a warning and migrated to the new key on the next write (tomlkit, B-uni-fsio-toml). Apply this to every rename P-unify makes: doc->docs, rules->rule (alias), schedule naming, search --source, and any MCP tool renames. The parity test treats an alias as its canonical command. Tests: each alias works, notices once, is hidden from listings, and suggestions are made.
data.title: Aliases and deprecations in the shared command registry and knob metadata: old command, flag, MCP tool, argument and config key names keep working with a one-line notice until 1.0; 'did you mean' for unknown names; the D-unify renames go through it

data.body: Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). Today a Claude/Gemini settings hook is recognised by its subcommand substring ('hooks session-start'), and the git hook's HOOK_MARKER v1 is never compared. Renaming a subcommand would orphan the old hook, add a duplicate and commit a failing command. Give every hook and managed entry a stable ownership marker independent of the command text ('ddflow-hook id=session-start fmt=N'), and add a migration (B-uni-compat-migrations) that recognises the legacy substring form once. The scanner parses each artifact type and resolves each reference: ok, deprecated (alias, with the replacement), or unknown. Doctor lists findings with file:line. upgrade --apply rewrites references only inside ddflow-managed regions and files, with a backup. User-owned text gets a proposed patch, never a silent edit.
data.title: Stale references in projects: find every ddflow command and ddflow_* tool named in adopted artifacts (settings hooks, git hooks, pre-commit config, driver docs, AGENTS/CLAUDE blocks, slash commands, ejected prompts and mcp_instructions, macros), check them against the registry and aliases, report deprecated or unknown ones, and rewrite ddflow-managed ones on upgrade

data.body: Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). One header or marker on every managed file and region, in the D-doc-regions grammar extended with ddflow=<version> fmt=<FORMAT_LEVEL> sha=<body digest>. Files covered: exports (whose v= is never compared today), adopted docs and blocks, .ddflow/.gitignore, git hooks, the rules view and generated views. Writers compare the header: same level -> normal; written by a newer level -> keep every part this version does not understand and refuse only a write that would downgrade or lose newer content (exit 3, 'upgrade ddflow to >= X'), per D-compat (2); hand-edited -> the D-doc-regions merge. rules_status and driver_drift stop calling every difference 'from an older version'. adopt --refresh-docs backs up before writing (B-upgrade.4 backups). Tests: an older writer meets a newer file in each artifact type.
data.title: Every file ddflow writes says which ddflow wrote it, and an older ddflow never downgrades it: version and format headers on managed files, newer/older/hand-edited told apart instead of byte equality, unknown parts preserved, refusal only on a direct conflict

data.body: Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). Payloads stay append-only: the log is never rewritten. Each kind declares a payload version (v in data, default 1). core/upcasters maps (kind, v) to a pure function returning the current shape, and the fold applies it before the handler. A snapshot of every kind with its fields and types is committed (tests/fixtures/event_kinds.json). A removed kind, a removed field or a changed type fails the test unless an upcaster is registered and the contract doc names the change. One malformed event no longer aborts the fold: it is recorded as a fold problem (event id, kind, error), shown in doctor, and the fold continues (strict mode still raises for tests). Unknown kinds from a newer ddflow are counted and preserved, as today. Fixtures: real logs from several released versions (B-uni-compat-tests).
data.title: Event evolution: per-kind payload versions, a registry of pure upcasters applied when the log is read, a fold isolated per event, and a ratchet that refuses a removed or retyped event field without an upcaster

data.body: Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). The fingerprint is a hash of the fold and projection modules, SCHEMA, textsim.VERSION and FORMAT_LEVEL. A projection change no longer depends on someone remembering a bump. The index becomes index-<fingerprint>.db; the newest is used and stale ones are garbage-collected after N days. Every LocalStore file carries a format version. A reader that meets a newer format ignores it and rebuilds what is derivable; for user data such as quotas.json it reads the fields it knows and preserves the rest. It never raises QuotaError the way quota.py:209 does today. Tests: two worktrees on different fingerprints, and an old reader against a new store.
data.title: Derived and local stores keyed on what built them: a code fingerprint for index.db and the read snapshot instead of the manual SCHEMA constant, one index per fingerprint so worktrees on different versions stop rebuilding each other's, and versioned local stores that an older ddflow ignores and rebuilds rather than refuses

data.body: Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). Today config --set and ddflow_configure validate the whole resulting file non-leniently, so an older ddflow cannot change any setting once a newer knob exists (R-upgrade-experiment). Change this: validate the keys being written plus every key this version knows; unknown keys and sections pass through byte-identical. Make checked list knobs whose value set grows (dedupe.kinds, agent.routers, trailer_waivers) tolerant: an unknown member is ignored with a note, never a brick. Add knob metadata renamed_from / default_changed_in / removed_in, applied at load and on write, with D-upgrade-config-changes confirmation for operator-set values. Add an optional config 'format = N' at the top and treat a newer format as D-compat (2). Make doctor's advice depend on install_info: 'merge main' only for a source tree, otherwise the upgrade command for the install method.
data.title: Config across versions: an older ddflow changes the keys it knows and keeps newer keys untouched instead of refusing the file; enum lists tolerate unknown members; renamed keys migrate; a config format version; upgrade advice that fits how ddflow is installed

data.body: Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). Today the skew guard keys only on __version__. A branch or source tree that adds kinds without a bump, every patch release, and unpinned MCP entries slip through. Add a ddflow.capabilities event: the first write that uses a capability records it, like git's repository format extensions. A writer then checks the capabilities a write needs against the ones it has. Examples: minting an id under a configured template it cannot render, writing a rule while rules are events, appending under a redaction profile it lacks. Only that write is refused (D-compat 2), with the version that provides the capability; everything else proceeds. Dedupe and definition digests are computed on normalized text (whitespace, case, and redaction markers mapped to one token), so clones on different redaction profiles reach the same match. The skew guard also compares FORMAT_LEVEL. Tests: an older capability set against a newer log, for each capability.
data.title: Mixed-version clones: the log records the capabilities and format level its data needs (rules as events, redaction v2, id templates, marker grammar), an older writer that lacks a needed capability is refused just that write, and digests that decide duplicates or definitions are computed on a normalized form

data.body: Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). Results gain a top-level 'schema': '<command>@<n>'. Field removal or retyping bumps n and keeps the old shape available for one minor release through --json-schema <n>. The registry generates the JSON Schema per command (shared with the MCP outputSchema). syrupy goldens pin each shape, and the release check (B-uni-compat-contract) compares them with the previous release.
data.title: A contract for machine-readable output: every --json and MCP structured result names its schema and version, fields are additive within a version, and snapshots catch any undeclared change

data.body: Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). This builds on B-upgrade.2-.5: the manifest, plan, apply and the versioned-repairs registry. Each migration declares since_version, format_level, the artifact kinds it touches, and four functions: detect (pure), plan (a dry-run diff), apply (backup first, writes only through fsio, any log change as corrective events, idempotent) and verify. B-uni-rules-import, the marker-dialect migration from D-doc-regions, the hook-marker migration (B-uni-compat-refs) and the reference rewrites are registered here and are not implemented ad hoc. upgrade --plan lists the pending migrations; --apply runs them per category with consent (D-upgrade-model pieces as accepted). Tests: every migration on fixture projects from older versions is idempotent and verifies.
data.title: One migration registry that P-unify's own breaking changes use: rules files to events, one marker grammar, hook ownership markers, doc to docs references, the redaction profile, tomlkit write-back and id templates, each with detect, plan, apply (backed up, idempotent, append-only events) and verify, run by ddflow upgrade

data.body: Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). Generate fixtures by installing released wheels (0.1.3, 0.1.10, 0.1.15, 0.1.18 and the current release) into throwaway venvs, building a small project with each, and committing the logs, config and adopted files. Tests: (1) new reads old: the golden folded state and replay are identical, and upgrade --apply makes every migration verify; (2) old reads new: an old wheel against a project written by the new release refuses only conflicting writes, preserves unknown parts, and never crashes; (3) surface snapshots (--help tree, tools/list, JSON schemas, config --explain, event-kind registry) are diffed against the previous release, and every difference must be declared in the manifest. The matrix runs in CI (slow marker) and in release.sh.
data.title: Compatibility test matrix: fixture projects, logs and configs from released versions, golden folds, runs of an old release against new data and of the new release against old data, and surface snapshots compared with the previous release

data.body:
A machine-readable manifest shipped in the wheel (ddflow/templates/upgrade/changes.toml) listing per release: new knobs (key, default, one-line why), CHANGED defaults (knob, old, new, behaviour effect), instruction/hook/template refreshes, repairs (ids), and opt-in features with the enabling command. Generated at release time from the log's complete --changelog lines + a lint that fails the release when config.py gained/changed a knob not listed (the dedupe warn->ask flip would have been caught). Reader API: changes_since(version).
Failing-first: a test diffs KNOB defaults between the previous tag and HEAD and requires a manifest entry for each added/changed knob; reading since 0.1.3 returns the 20 knobs found in the experiment. Docs shipped in templates; README section.

OPERATOR DECISION D-upgrade-manifest-lint (2026-10-03): the manifest lint BLOCKS a release by default ([release].manifest_lint = block|warn|off, default block, via config/CLI/MCP). A block prints the unmanifested changes and the operator's options: have an agent prepare the missing entries and safe-upgrade notes (pre-filled from the changelog fields and knob diff), waive named entries for this release with --waive <change> --reason (recorded), or change the policy. Agents may prepare and propose; waiving or lowering the policy is the operator's call. Failing-first test: a new knob with no entry blocks and prints the three options; a prepared entry passes; a waiver is recorded and shown in the next plan; warn and off do not block.

D-compat (operator 2026-10-06): part of P-unify's finish line (B-uni-acceptance needs it); P-unify's breaking changes are applied through it (B-uni-compat-migrations).

`ddflow upgrade` (default = --plan, writes nothing, exit 0 up to date / 2 nothing to do vs 1 plan pending per exit-code convention), MCP ddflow_upgrade (plan and apply args), and `ddflow doctor --upgrade` as an alias. The plan reports by category: data repairs available, config (new knobs, changed defaults that alter this project's behaviour because it has no entry), instructions (driver docs / rules blocks / native rules whose bytes differ, hand-edited ones flagged separately), hooks (git hooks pointing at a missing or different binary, missing SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit hooks), MCP launch, newly available opt-in features and `ddflow companions`. Reuses driver_drift/rules_status, hooks status, Config source tracking, manifest.
Failing-first: against the 0.1.3-built fixture project the plan lists the missing UserPromptSubmit hook, drifted driver doc, dedupe/readme knobs, a dangling pre-commit binary; against a fresh init it is empty. Plan output byte-identical in CLI --json and MCP.

OPERATOR DECISION D-upgrade-config-changes (2026-10-03): agents may apply upgrade config changes where the project never set the value; any value the operator set (present in any config layer, env, or set via ddflow config/ddflow_configure) is never changed without the operator's confirmation: the plan marks it 'needs operator confirmation', --apply refuses it unless --confirm <knob> --reason is passed and is recorded; changed shipped defaults are always listed in the plan, notice and upgrade.applied. [upgrade].config_changes = agent|ask|operator (default agent). Failing-first test: an operator-set knob whose default/name changed is refused without --confirm, applied with it; an unset knob is applied by the agent; both appear in the plan.

D-compat (operator 2026-10-06): part of P-unify's finish line (B-uni-acceptance needs it); P-unify's breaking changes are applied through it (B-uni-compat-migrations).

--apply <category,...>|all. Before ANY write: snapshot every file it will touch to .ddflow/backups/<ts>-<from>-to-<to>/ (local, git-ignored) and print the git diff command; driver docs and rules blocks get a version+body-sha256 header (like export docs) so hand edits are detected and the file is moved aside (.local-edits) or refused, never silently overwritten (also fix adopt --refresh-docs to use it). Dangling git-hook binary is repaired by hooks install. Idempotent: second apply is a no-op. Appends upgrade.applied (from, to, categories, backup) so replay explains it. Config-default changes are never auto-applied: they are listed with 'pin old behaviour: ddflow config --set X old' and recorded when the operator acknowledges.
Failing-first: local edit in driver doc survives to .local-edits and is reported; apply twice = identical tree; kill mid-apply leaves backup and a re-runnable plan; replay shows the upgrade event.

OPERATOR DECISION D-upgrade-backups (2026-10-03): backups are LOCAL by default ([upgrade].backup = local|snapshot|none, default local, .ddflow/backups git-ignored, [upgrade].backup_keep); a git-tracked snapshot is the opt-in (--snapshot or [upgrade].backup = snapshot; refused clearly on a dirty tree or without git); `ddflow upgrade --restore <backup>`; configurable via config, CLI and MCP. README MUST explain both options, the default, what each costs and how to restore (acceptance: a test asserts the README section exists and names both).

A registry of repairs, each {id, since_version, detect(state, log) -> findings, repair(findings) -> corrective events, test fixture}. Run by upgrade/doctor; never rewrites history; applied repairs are recorded (repair.applied id) so they are not re-offered. Seed set from this week's fixes: unadopted orphan prompts/notes (session adopt-orphans), item completed FORCED over unmet gates (report, annotate), shards by an agent with no history, torn/mismatched-id lines (report + quarantine note, no deletion), and stale exported documents carrying an old render (export refresh). data.claim: Decisions are an ADR-shaped log record (core/records.py:632: title, context, decision, consequences, alternatives, globs, tags, sources, status proposed|accepted|superseded, decided_by, supersedes) with add/list/show/search/applicable/supersede on CLI and MCP, recall and DECISIONS.md export, ADR import from docs/adr. Reminder exists only in brief/claim by glob overlap (api/lifecycle/brief.py:104-112). Gaps: (1) advisory only -- no checks that code follows a decision (no fitness functions); (2) review gates (rubber_duck, critic, standards) do not receive governing decisions; no commit-time or periodic check; (3) no category, owner, enforcement level, review date or revisit trigger; statuses lack deprecated/retired/rejected; (4) no dependency/library policy (allow, forbid, version ranges, tech-radar ring) checked when a manifest changes; (5) no violation workflow: no waivers with expiry and approval; (6) no staleness review; (7) no edit/retire (B199 plans a generic one), no file-authored decisions; (8) no presets (stack packs) and no inference of current decisions from an existing codebase; (9) ADR files are imported once, never kept in sync. Planned work covering slices: B199, B-path-rules-to-decisions, B-architecture-pass (default style decision, generated layer rules), B-coh-contradiction, B-rw-vs-decision, B-semantic-recall, B-provenance-remaining-surfaces, B-uni-def-records, B-uni-record-surface, B-dt-library (ADR collection), P-org-config (company decisions), B-sched-defaults (architecture review job).

data.mechanism: Prior art: ADRs (Nygard, MADR statuses incl. deprecated and review dates, adr-tools, log4brains), architectural fitness functions (Ford, Parsons, Kua: Building Evolutionary Architectures), ArchUnit, import-linter, dependency-cruiser and Semgrep rules as executable decisions, Thoughtworks/Backstage Tech Radar rings (adopt/trial/assess/hold) for library policy, Renovate packageRules and deptry for dependency policy, OPA/conftest for config assertions, Danger-style PR-time checks, CODEOWNERS for decision owners, exception/waiver registers with expiry (security programmes).

data.question: How should ddflow keep, preset, monitor and maintain a project's architectural decisions (infrastructure, coding style, libraries, dependencies, upgrade policy, tests, security) so they are checked and reminded wherever they apply, and managed like every other record (CLI, MCP, config, add/edit/remove, search, RAG)?

data.body: Operator 2026-10-06 (verbatim in session s20260929T144138-2948413): keep and maintain architectural decisions for every project, let the user preset them, let ddflow remind and monitor them wherever they apply, manageable like the rest (CLI, config, add, remove, edit, search, RAG), so decisions about infrastructure, way of coding, libraries, dependencies, upgrades and tests are monitored and maintained per project. Research R-decisions (CONFIRMED). TODAY: a small ADR record (globs, alternatives, supersede-only) reminded in brief/claim by glob overlap; no checks, no review-gate injection, no category/owner/enforcement/review date, no dependency policy, no waivers, no staleness review, no edit or retire, no presets, no inference, ADR files imported once. DESIGN: a decision is a record (on the definition-record model, B-uni-def-records) with category, scope globs, owner, enforcement (advisory|warn|block), review_by and revisit triggers, links, and CHECKS: fitness functions of typed kinds (deps, imports, pattern, files, config, command, radar) evaluated by one engine on the tree or a diff, unavailable never passed. Monitoring points: brief and claim (reminder), review gate prompts (reviewers verify compliance), a task-level 'decisions' gate (mechanical checks on the diff), pre-commit fast checks (manifests, staged files), a periodic sweep job (drift report) and event triggers (manifest changed, decision accepted). A violation is fixed, waived (scoped, time-boxed, approved) or answered with a superseding proposal for the operator. Presets: shipped and company decision packs applied with an interview; onboarding infers current decisions from the codebase as proposals. Every operation on CLI, MCP, a /decide prompt and authored files (.ddflow/decisions/*.toml); recall/search/context packs include decisions; ADR files kept in sync through the ADR document type. BUILDS ON (does not duplicate): B199 (generic edit/retire; this phase extends it for decisions), B-path-rules-to-decisions, B-architecture-pass, B-coh-contradiction, B-rw-vs-decision, B-semantic-recall, B-provenance-remaining-surfaces, B-uni-def-records, B-uni-record-surface, B-uni-cmdrunner, B-uni-approval, B-uni-context-pack, B-uni-kind-pipeline, B-uni-triggers, B-dt-library (ADR collection), P-org-config (company packs, enforced decisions), B-sched-defaults (architecture review job), B-dependency-upgrades. Waits for P-unify (D-unify-first). Order: decide -> model -> {manage, checks} -> {deps, monitor, review, rag} -> waivers -> presets -> {infer, adr-files} -> acceptance.
data.title: Architectural decisions as maintained, checked infrastructure: categories, owners and review dates; executable checks and dependency policy; reminders in brief, reviews, commits and periodic sweeps; waivers; presets and inference; managed on every surface

data.body: Ask the operator, record D-decision-management, and write the doc. Recommended defaults: categories architecture, infrastructure, coding-style, libraries, dependencies, upgrade, testing, security, data, process (extensible); enforcement warn by default, block opt-in per decision; an agent may propose but only a person accepts (status proposed -> accepted); a waiver needs operator approval and expires within 90 days at most; command checks only from operator config or approved by digest (D-doc-types pattern); shipped packs python-library, python-service, web-frontend, go-service, container-infra, testing-baseline, security-baseline, upgrade-policy; ADR files kept in two-way sync through the ADR document type.

Statuses gain deprecated, retired and rejected; live means accepted. Every change is recorded through B-uni-def-records (recorded, updated, retired, superseded), and an upcaster (B-uni-compat-events) maps existing decision.recorded events with no loss. data.body: Built on the record surface (B-uni-record-surface) so CLI and MCP bodies are identical. It covers B199's decision part, coordinated with B199 rather than duplicated. Filters: category, status, owner, glob, stale, enforcement, with-checks. Authored files are .ddflow/decisions/<id>.toml, read through the overlay loader and imported by digest the way rules are (D-unify 7), so a team can keep decisions in review-friendly files. A hand edit becomes an event, and an older ddflow preserves unknown fields (D-compat). The add-time duplicate and contradiction check covers decisions (B-coh-contradiction). An agent's add is status proposed; acceptance is a person's act (B-uni-approval), per D-decision-management.
data.title: Manage decisions like every record: add, edit (including clearing a field), accept, reject, deprecate, retire, supersede, list with filters, show, history, search and applicable, on CLI, MCP, a /decide prompt and authored .ddflow/decisions/*.toml files

data.body:
Each kind is a pure evaluator returning pass, fail or unavailable, with file:line findings and a digest.
- deps: allow and forbid lists plus version ranges against parsed manifests (pyproject/requirements, package.json, go.mod, Cargo.toml, Gemfile, basic pom/gradle; stdlib parsers).
- imports: layer and forbidden-import contracts, using import-linter or dependency-cruiser when the project configures them (an adapter, unavailable when absent), otherwise a simple import scan for Python and JS/TS.
- pattern: required or forbidden regex, or a Semgrep rule when semgrep is configured, over the decision's globs.
- files: must or must not exist.
- config: assert a key in TOML, JSON, YAML or INI files, or a ddflow knob value.
- command: an operator-configured command run through B-uni-cmdrunner with digest approval; exit 0 passes.
- radar: see B-dec-deps.
Results are cached per tree fingerprint. Tests cover each kind, plus the unavailable path.
data.title: Executable decisions: one fitness-function engine with typed checks -- deps, imports, pattern, files, config, command, radar -- evaluated on the whole tree or a diff, with locations, and unavailable never counted as passed

data.body: Radar entries are decision-linked records, or a section of a decision. A diff that adds or changes a dependency is checked: forbidden or hold fails at the decision's enforcement level; a dependency the radar does not know raises a 'needs a decision' finding (warn by default). data.decision: Operator 2026-10-07, after measurement (34 fixes since 2026-10-06 12:00 UTC: median 62 min each; per fix about 2.1 full-suite unit_tests runs at 12 min, 2.9 rubber_duck and 2.9 critic rounds with about 65% failing, mostly on findings later refuted, and 2.2 ci runs). (1) A bug fix or small task runs only the selected tests in unit_tests (ddflow tests --item: tests for the changed files plus the regression test); the full suite runs once, in ci, on the final merge result, and a failure there still blocks the merge. (2) A change under about 150 changed lines gets ONE cross-family review whose prompt covers both rubber_duck and critic, and that outcome is recorded for both gates. Larger changes keep both reviews. At most 2 full rounds; after that, remaining findings are triaged, and the gate is passed-on-refutation (flagged, D-unify 5) or escalated to the operator. (3) A re-review always sends the item's full diff against its base, together with the previous findings and their triage, never only the newest commits.

data.body: Make D-gate-economy (1) the default workflow, not a convention. For fix tasks and small tasks (a size threshold knob), the unit_tests gate runs the tests selected by testselect: the tests for the changed files plus the declared regression test. The evidence lists which tests ran and why. The ci gate runs the full suite on the merge result before merge. Knobs: [gates] unit_tests_scope = selected|full per kind, default selected for fix and small tasks. A selection that cannot be computed falls back to the full suite and says so.

data.body: For a diff under [review].combined_under_lines (default 150), ddflow review --gate rubber_duck,critic sends ONE request whose prompt covers both lenses and records the outcome for both gates, with the shared review id in evidence. Larger diffs keep both reviews, run in parallel. The round limit (max_rounds 2) also bounds delta rounds. After it, the gate is passed-on-refutation (flagged, D-unify 5) when every finding has a probe, or escalated to the operator.

data.body: Today a delta round often sees only the follow-up commit and reports 'fix absent'. A re-review sends the full item diff against its base (bug fixes are small), plus a compact list of the previous findings with their triage (confirmed and fixed, or refuted with the probe), and asks the reviewer to confirm each and look for new issues. Delta-only remains available, with --delta-only, for very large diffs.
